    AI Overview
    Immunization is
    the process of making a person resistant to infectious diseases, typically via vaccines that stimulate the immune system to recognize and fight pathogens like bacteria or viruses. It is a critical, highly effective public health tool that prevents 3.5–5 million deaths annually, protecting against diseases like measles, COVID-19, and tetanus. 
    How It Works & Types 
    • Active Immunization (Vaccines): Introduces a weakened, inactive, or partial germ (mRNA, protein subunits) to teach the body to produce antibodies without causing the disease.
    • Passive Immunization: Provides immediate protection by giving antibodies directly (e.g., immunoglobulins) rather than relying on the body to produce them.
    • Types of Vaccines: Included are live-attenuated (measles/mumps/rubella), inactivated (polio), subunit/conjugate (HPV, Hib), and mRNA (some COVID-19). 
    Purpose & Benefits 
    • Individual Protection: Prepares the immune system for future exposure, reducing the risk of severe illness or death.
    • Herd Immunity: Protects vulnerable populations who cannot be vaccinated (e.g., infants, immunocompromised) by limiting the disease spread in the community.
    • Disease Eradication: Has eliminated or significantly reduced diseases like smallpox and polio. 
    Side Effects & Safety 
    • Vaccines are safe and thoroughly tested.
    • Common, mild side effects: Pain, swelling, or redness at the injection site, low-grade fever, headache, and fatigue. These are temporary and signs the body is building protection. 
    Common Vaccinations 
    • Children: DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis), MMR, Polio, Hib, Varicella, Hepatitis B.
    • Adults: Influenza, COVID-19, Shingles, Tdap. 
    For a personalized schedule or to check for specific risks, it is best to consult with a medical provider.

    What does immunization mean?
    Immunization is the process whereby a person is made resistant to a disease, typically by the administration of a vaccine. Vaccines stimulate the body's own immune system to protect the person against subsequent infection or disease.

    Purpose. What is the purpose of immunization?
    About this result
    Feedback
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    The purpose of immunization (vaccination) is to train your immune system to recognize and fight specific, harmful diseases before you're exposed, preventing illness, severe complications, or death by building resistance safely through weakened germs, making it a cornerstone of public health for individuals and communities. It protects vulnerable people (like infants) and can even lead to disease eradication through herd immunity.
     
    How it works
    • Mimics infection: Vaccines introduce a harmless version (weakened, killed, or parts) of a virus or bacteria to your body, tricking your immune system into thinking it's a real infection. 
    • Builds immunity: Your body creates antibodies and memory cells to fight the germ, just as it would with a natural infection, but without getting sick. 
    • Provides future protection: If you encounter the real disease later, your immune system "remembers" it and can quickly destroy it before it causes illness. 
    Key benefits
    • Prevents serious illness: Protects against diseases that can cause long-term disability or death. 
    • Safer than disease: Vaccination is far safer than getting the actual infection. 
    • Community protection (Herd Immunity): When enough people are vaccinated, it stops the disease from spreading, protecting those who can't be vaccinated (like newborns or the immunocompromised). 
    • Reduces outbreaks: Fewer sick people means less strain on hospitals and better care for everyone.

      Side Effects. What are the side effects of immunization?
      About this result
      Feedback
      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      Immunization side effects are usually mild, temporary signs your immune system is working, like soreness, redness, or swelling at the injection site, mild fever, fatigue, headache, or fussiness, lasting a couple of days. Serious reactions are very rare but can happen, requiring immediate medical help, such as severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis), symptoms of which include difficulty breathing or swelling of the face/throat.
       
      Common, Mild Side Effects (Usually a few hours to days)
      • At the Injection Site: Pain, redness, swelling, or tenderness.
      • Body-Wide: Low-grade fever, chills, headache, muscle aches, fatigue, nausea, fussiness (in babies), or feeling sleepy. 
      • Delayed Reactions: With some vaccines like MMR, a mild rash or swollen glands can appear 1-4 weeks later. 
      Less Common & Serious Side Effects (Very Rare)
      • Febrile Seizures: A small risk in young children, often linked to fever after vaccination. 
      • Anaphylaxis (Severe Allergy): Symptoms like hives, swelling of the face/throat, wheezing, rapid heart rate, or dizziness can occur minutes to hours after vaccination and need urgent treatment. 
      What to Do
      • For mild symptoms: Cool washcloth on the sore spot, fluids, rest, or fever reducers (like acetaminophen or ibuprofen, if appropriate). 
      • For serious symptoms: Seek immediate medical attention or call emergency services. 
      • Report concerns: Contact your healthcare provider for advice on any worrying reactions.
